heading: From a Kakatiya mud fort to a Nizam's capital
body: Telangana's history pivots on a single fortress that changed hands and purpose again and again. Golconda began as a simple mud fort built in the 11th century by the Hindu Kakatiya dynasty, who ruled the Telugu-speaking Deccan from their capital at Warangal. The Kakatiyas ceded the fort to the Bahmani Sultanate in 1363, and when the Bahmani kingdom fragmented in the early 16th century, one of its Turkish governors, Quli Qutb Shah, declared independence in 1518 and made Golconda the seat of a new Qutb Shahi dynasty — even though the family's own origins were Persian, their rule became closely identified with Telugu language and culture over the next two centuries.

By the late 16th century Golconda had outgrown its fort, and Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah founded a new planned capital a few miles away: Hyderabad. The Qutb Shahi dynasty ruled until 1687, when the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb annexed Golconda after a long siege and ended the line of independent Deccan sultanates his empire had spent decades fighting. Mughal control did not last: the governor Asaf Jah declared his own independence from a weakening Mughal court in 1713, taking the title Nizam-ul-Mulk, and the Nizams he founded ruled Hyderabad State as one of British India's largest princely states until 1948, when the Indian government's police action ended their rule three years after independence.

That layered succession — Hindu Kakatiya fort, Persian-descended but Telugu-rooted Qutb Shahi sultanate, then Mughal-descended Nizam state — is why Telangana's historical sites look so different from temple-dominated Tamil Nadu or Karnataka: Golconda's fortifications, the Qutb Shahi tombs, and Hyderabad's Charminar and palaces belong to an unusually continuous run of Deccan Muslim rule layered directly on top of a Hindu warrior-dynasty's foundations.
The map entries for Telangana follow that same arc, from the Kakatiya fort walls at the base of Golconda through the Qutb Shahi capital to the Nizam-era city that Hyderabad became.
